page.about.heading: The GPT-6 Astra star field, rebuilt as mathematics
page.about.lede: Five Bézier strokes, about 4,600 stars streaming toward the core, and a scattered sky that gathers into shape. Every number behind it is a parameter you can move in the full-screen demo.
page.about.preview_hint: Running live from the same parameters. Click to open it full screen.
page.about.gpt6_p1: GPT-6 Astra is the model OpenAI announced on 3 September 2026, first as a limited preview and then, the following day, to paid ChatGPT users and the API. OpenAI describes it as its most capable and most aligned model to date.
page.about.gpt6_p2: The largest gains it claims are in agentic work: operating a computer, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity and science, including several agents working together on long tasks. It is also the first model OpenAI rated at its “critical” cybersecurity level, which is why it rolled out in stages.
page.about.gpt6_p3: This site is not about the model. It is about the star field on its announcement page, and about what can be learned by taking that piece apart.
page.about.disclaimer: An independent study project, not affiliated with or endorsed by OpenAI. GPT-6 and Astra are OpenAI’s names; none of their code is used here.
entry.astra.title: GPT-6 Astra · the spiral field
entry.astra.tagline: Five Bézier strokes of stars, streaming inward
entry.astra.summary: The hero of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra page is a galaxy of about 4,600 points. Its five arms are Bézier strokes read from a small SVG, the stars stream along them toward the core, and the whole field first appears scattered across the screen before swinging into place.
astra.hint: Drag to tilt the star field; it settles back when you let go.
astra.m.glyph.title: Five strokes, not a spiral formula
astra.m.glyph.vars: B_k the k-th cubic Bézier stroke of a 231 × 325 SVG · c its centre (114.973, 211.36) · u arc-length fraction along the stroke · d_k per-stroke depth amplitude · D depth relief · H how much of the viewport height the glyph spans
astra.m.glyph.note: No spiral equation produces this shape. The arms are five hand-drawn Bézier strokes in a small SVG, mapped to world units by 9.7/325 and shown in a frame 10.9 units tall with the camera lifted 1.2 units, so the core sits 11% below the middle of the viewport. Each stroke is resampled by arc length into 512 points; the z relief only shows when you tilt the field.
astra.m.stars.title: Scattering stars along a stroke
astra.m.stars.vars: i uniform position along the stroke · U how strongly stars crowd toward the middle · w(s) the width at that point · σ arm width · u, u₁, u₂ uniform random numbers · δ across-stroke offset, triangular · N_k stars on stroke k (220 or 170 per unit of density) · N_bg extra stars left in the sky
astra.m.stars.note: A uniform position is bent toward the middle of the stroke by a sine term, so both ends thin out. The across-stroke offset is triangular, not Gaussian, and its width follows the same sine: narrow at the tips, up to σ in the middle. Three of the five strokes are “strong” and get 220 stars per unit of density, the other two 170.
astra.m.hero.title: Hero stars
astra.m.hero.vars: h_k chance of a hero star on stroke k (8.5% strong, 5.5% weak), scaled by the same sine · S star size · ⌀ point scale before the pixel mapping · L brightness · N total stars · the largest star of each stroke is raised further and becomes a lens-flare source
astra.m.hero.note: Most stars are small: size 0.12 + 0.68·u^2.4 keeps them near the floor. A few percent are hero stars, five to seven times bigger and two to three times brighter, and they carry the look. Weak strokes are dimmed to 82%. This is why the field reads as crowded pinpoints with a handful of bright beads, not as a uniform dust.
astra.m.color.title: Five colours by threshold
astra.m.color.vars: u a uniform draw from a second random stream · c₀…c₄ light blue, blue, orange, light orange, white · E the energy boost for saturated colours · I intensity
astra.m.color.note: 36% light blue, 16% blue, 12% orange, 10% light orange, 26% white. Colours come from their own random stream so changing the geometry never reshuffles them. Saturated colours are boosted by up to 42% in energy, and bright stars whiten from the centre out, which is why the big ones look white with a coloured rim.
astra.m.core.title: The core cluster
astra.m.core.vars: r radius, concentrated by u^2.4 · θ angle · the cluster is squashed to 72% vertically · L brightness, highest at the centre · N_c stars in the cluster · Ω rigid spin, 0.36 × flow speed · T_c one turn
astra.m.core.note: The core is not a glow painted on top; it is about a hundred real stars packed into a radius of 0.42 units, elliptical, brightest and whitest in the middle, rendered 22% hotter than the arms. The cluster turns as a rigid body in the same direction the arms flow, and the lens flare sits on its brightest member.
astra.m.flow.title: Streaming inward
astra.m.flow.vars: φ_k phase of a star on stroke k · ω_k the stroke’s own rate in turns per second (0.025, 0.018, 0.021, 0.016, 0.03), signed toward the core · v flow speed · τ(t) time with the entrance gate integrated · vis fade at both ends · T_k seconds for one star to cross stroke k · ṡ_k its speed in world units per second · t_flow when the flow starts
astra.m.flow.note: Nothing rotates as a pattern. Each star keeps a phase along its stroke and the phase advances at a constant rate, so every star moves at constant speed along the curve and the angular rate falls off as 1/r on the round parts. The sign is chosen per stroke so that motion always heads for the end nearer the core. Stars fade over the last 5.5% at each end, and the flow only opens once the entrance is 55% done.
astra.m.twinkle.title: Twinkle
astra.m.twinkle.vars: a amplitude of the brightness swing · φ a phase per star · ω twinkle rate · ρ a rate per star between 0.65 and 1.35 · the point size follows with 3%, the opacity with 8%
astra.m.twinkle.note: A slow sine, not a flicker: at ω = 0.62 a star takes ten seconds or more to breathe once. It moves the brightness by ±14% and the size by only ±3%, so the field shimmers without ever seeming to blink. Like the flow, it stays frozen until the entrance is more than half done.
astra.m.reveal.title: The entrance: scattered, then gathered
astra.m.reveal.vars: A entrance progress from 0 to 1 · t₀ delay before it starts · T its length · δ a tiny per-star delay · r(A) how far a star has emerged (its size is √r, it is fully opaque once r reaches 0.2) · P_sky its random start position across 112% of the viewport · P_arm its place on the stroke · pull a smoothed ramp that starts between 14% and 32% and lasts 58% to 68% of T · R(θ) a swing of up to 0.66 rad around the centre while it travels
astra.m.reveal.note: The first thing you see is not a galaxy but a sky: within the first 14% of the entrance every star has faded in at 45% size, spread randomly over the whole viewport. Then, star by star, each one starts its pull toward its place on the stroke, swinging around the centre on the way and growing to full size. The 12% extra background stars never leave the sky. There is no fade-to-black at the end; the flow and the twinkle simply switch on as the last stars arrive.
astra.m.optics.title: The shape of a point
astra.m.optics.vars: d normalised distance from the point centre · core the dome every star is drawn with · ray the cross that only stars brighter than 1.45 receive · x, y normalised offsets · ⌀ the star’s scale · ⌀₀ base diameter, ⌀₁ diameter per unit of scale, both in CSS pixels · points thinner than 4 px are drawn with a cubic filter so they never vanish
astra.m.optics.note: Star sizes are in CSS pixels and do not scale with the viewport: on a small window the galaxy shrinks but the stars do not, which is why the same field looks denser on a laptop than on a large display. A star is a dome raised to 2.2, a bright one gets a faint cross, and the very small ones are anti-aliased with a cubic B-spline so a 1 px star still contributes energy proportional to its area.
astra.m.tonemap.title: Bloom and ACES
astra.m.tonemap.vars: C linear light summed in a float buffer · Y its luminance · θ bloom threshold, smoothed over 0.18 · mip_j five successive half-resolution levels, blended back with radius r · G a final 9-tap Gaussian · I_b bloom intensity · ACES the filmic curve at exposure 1, applied after dividing by 0.6 · sRGB the display encoding
astra.m.tonemap.note: Light is summed linearly in a half-float buffer; nothing is blended in display space. Almost everything passes the 0.08 threshold, so the bloom is not a highlight effect but a soft veil that gives each arm its haze. ACES then compresses the core to white and keeps the mid-tones coloured. The offline renderer runs the same chain with Pillow, so poster, GIF and video are the same picture as the page.
astra.m.flare.title: Lens flare
astra.m.flare.vars: d aspect-corrected distance from the core in viewport units · h halo strength · s streak strength · c the core’s screen position, ghosts placed along the line to the centre · I_f overall flare intensity · the brightest star of each stroke is a secondary source at 55% strength
astra.m.flare.note: The wide soft glow around the core is mostly bloom; the flare adds the tight halo, a faint ring at 0.105, thin horizontal and vertical streaks and three small ghosts mirrored through the screen centre. Its strength is 0.28, deliberately restrained so that a tiny tracking error can never read as a second star.
astra.m.spin.title: Drag to tilt
astra.m.spin.vars: θ_x, θ_y the target tilt · κ radians per pixel of drag · Δp pointer movement · θ_k the tilt each stroke has actually reached · λ how fast it follows (14 while dragging, 5.5 while returning) · lag_k 0.18 + 0.17k, so outer strokes trail the inner ones · ρ how much of that lag applies
astra.m.spin.note: The field is a real 3D object: each stroke carries a sine relief in z, so tilting it parts the arms in depth. The strokes do not tilt together — each follows the pointer with its own lag, the outermost slowest, which makes the galaxy feel heavy. Release and everything springs back to face-forward at a slower rate.
astra.lang.palette: Black ground, a blue ambient veil in the corners, two blues, two oranges and one white. Nothing in between: every star is exactly one of five colours, and only saturation and bloom mix them on screen.
astra.lang.p1: Draw the shape by hand, then let mathematics populate it. Five Bézier strokes carry more intent than any spiral equation.
astra.lang.p2: Sum light linearly, bloom in linear space, tone-map once at the end. Never blend in display space.
astra.lang.p3: Hierarchy comes from a few hero stars, not from making everything brighter.
astra.lang.p4: The glyph must not move. Let the stars flow through it instead, each stroke at its own pace, always toward the core.
astra.lang.p5: Arrive from a sky, not from black. Scatter everything first, then gather it; the eye reads convergence as depth.
astra.lang.p6: Interaction is a tilt with weight: outer strokes lag, and everything returns to face-forward on release.
astra.origin.v1: The reference is the hero of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra announcement page, linked above.
astra.origin.v3: Frame-by-frame tracking of a screen recording confirms the model: stars stream inward along the strokes at constant speed, the core cluster turns rigidly, background stars stay put, and the entrance begins as a scattered sky.
astra.origin.r1: The implementation here is ours: WebGL2 and Canvas 2D written from scratch, not their code. The bloom, flare and dirt passes are approximations of the original post-processing chain, and the drag sensitivity and the short delay before the entrance are our choices.
astra.origin.r2: The flow speed default (1.3) is a calibration, not a derivation: it was set by tracking a screen recording, in which the stars stream about 1.6× faster than the value we started from.
